_meta.status: DECIDED AND APPLIED — repo artifacts and both live Notion option sets. Verified: every pre-existing option ID survived byte-identically; zero rows lost a value.
_meta.the_problem_it_fixed: Two disjoint department vocabularies existed on Sector-owned fields. `Sector Intelligence.Routed To` offered 5 values; `Sector Signals.Departments Affected` offered 7. Between them they could not name TEN departments Sector demonstrably routes to. The sharpest proof: DB 16 `Visual Language` states in its own Notion field description that it routes to Design (19) — a department neither vocabulary could express. A packet routed on one field could not be received by a workflow reading the other.
_meta.the_governing_rule: AEIT_06: 'departments consume canonical entities; they do not reinvent them.' GLOBAL_OS.md §4 IS the canonical department registry. The vocabulary is therefore not a Sector-curated subset — it is the registry itself. Curating a subset is exactly how the original two drifted apart, so a third curated subset would have repeated the failure.
_meta.naming_convention: Plain department names, taken VERBATIM from GLOBAL_OS.md §4. No numeric prefix. The department number is carried as `dept` metadata here, not inside the value string. Two reasons: (1) §4's names ARE the plain forms, so this is literally verbatim rather than a decorated variant; (2) it made the Notion migration purely additive — see `notion_migration.rename_is_destructive`.
_meta.scope_of_change: These two fields are the ONLY department-enum fields in any Notion schema across the whole repository (verified by grep over every *_SCHEMA.md and *_OS.md). No other department is affected.

notion_migration._status: APPLIED 2026-08-24. Both fields verified after the change.

rename_is_destructive._headline: A Notion select/multi-select option CANNOT be renamed through this DDL. `ALTER COLUMN … SET MULTI_SELECT(...)` matches options BY NAME: an option whose name changes is dropped and a new one created, and every row holding the old option loses that value.
rename_is_destructive._how_it_was_established: Empirically, before touching real data. A throwaway option `ZZ Migration Probe` was added to DB 7, its ID recorded, then the same ALTER was issued with the name changed to `ZZ Probe Renamed`. The ID changed from `MmE3MGFhMmYtY2NmYi00ZjQxLTkyYmQtMmRjNTU0YTdkNmFk` to `YzlmZTU0NDgtNWMzNy00YTZhLTllYTYtNzk3ZTNkN2UzZTk3`, proving drop-and-recreate. The 7 real options, whose names were unchanged in the same statements, kept their IDs throughout. The probe was then removed.
rename_is_destructive._what_it_prevented: The originally-planned migration used `NN Name` values (e.g. `Sales` → `05 Sales`), which would have renamed all 12 existing options across the two fields. Executed, it would have silently stripped the department values from every one of the 249 rows.
rename_is_destructive._the_rule_for_any_future_option_change: Adding options is safe. Removing an unused option is safe. RENAMING is a data migration, not a schema change — it requires re-tagging every affected row at page level first, or accepting the loss. Verify by comparing option IDs before and after, never by assuming.
rename_is_destructive._precedent_note: SECTOR_OS.md §15 (Gate 2) records ALTER COLUMN … SET SELECT operations where 'every option ID survived byte-identically'. That is consistent with this finding: those operations added options without renaming any.

notion_migration.method_used: ADD-ONLY. No option was renamed. Existing values were passed through unchanged, and the missing canonical values were appended.
